title: Making salts: preparing a pure, dry soluble salt
aim: To prepare a pure, dry sample of the soluble salt copper sulfate from the insoluble base copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
background: Soluble salts can be made by reacting an acid with an insoluble metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate. The solid is added to the acid until no more reacts. The salt formed depends on the acid: sulfuric acid makes sulfates, hydrochloric acid makes chlorides and nitric acid makes nitrates.

In this practical copper(II) oxide, a black insoluble base, reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to make blue copper sulfate solution and water: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l). The acid is warmed so the reaction is faster.

Copper oxide is added in excess so that all of the acid is used up. The unreacted copper oxide is then removed by filtration. The filtrate is a solution of copper sulfate only, which is heated to evaporate some of the water and then left to crystallise slowly, giving blue crystals of hydrated copper sulfate.

If a metal carbonate is used instead (for example copper carbonate with sulfuric acid), the method is the same but carbon dioxide is also given off, and fizzing stops when the acid is used up: CuCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
hypothesis: Adding excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid will neutralise all the acid and form copper sulfate solution, which will form blue copper sulfate crystals when it is concentrated and left to crystallise.

variables.independent: Not a fair-test investigation: this is a preparation. The key choice is the reactants (copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid), which decide the salt made.
variables.dependent: Mass and appearance of the copper sulfate crystals obtained (used to judge purity and yield).
control: Copper(II) oxide added in excess until no more dissolves
Temperature of the acid (warmed gently, not boiled)
Crystals left to form slowly at room temperature

equipment: Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze and heatproof mat
method: Use a measuring cylinder to add 40 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid to a 100 cm³ beaker.
Put the beaker on a tripod and gauze and heat the acid gently with a Bunsen burner until it is warm (about 50 °C). Do not let it boil. Turn off the Bunsen burner.
Use a spatula to add a small amount of copper(II) oxide powder to the warm acid and stir with a glass rod. The black solid dissolves and the solution turns blue.

Keep adding copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring each time, until some black solid remains and does not dissolve even after stirring. This shows the copper oxide is in excess and all the acid has reacted.
Let the mixture cool slightly, then set up a filter funnel lined with filter paper over a conical flask.
Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper(II) oxide. The black residue stays in the filter paper and the blue filtrate (copper sulfate solution) collects in the flask.
Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin. Heat it gently over a beaker of boiling water (a water bath) or directly with a low Bunsen flame to evaporate some of the water.
Stop heating when about half of the solution has evaporated, or when crystals start to form on a cold glass rod dipped into the solution and removed.
Pour the concentrated solution into a crystallising dish and leave it in a warm place for a few days so that the water evaporates slowly and large crystals form.
Remove the crystals and pat them dry between two pieces of filter paper, or leave them to dry in a warm place.
Weigh the dry crystals and record their mass and appearance.

safety.risk: Irritant to eyes and skin, especially when warm.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, use dilute acid and wash any splashes off skin immediately with plenty of water.

safety.risk: Harmful if swallowed; copper sulfate irritates eyes and skin and is toxic to aquatic life.
safety.precaution: Avoid skin contact, do not eat in the lab, wash hands afterwards and dispose of copper compounds in the waste container, not down the sink.

safety.hazard: Hot apparatus and spitting solution during evaporation
safety.risk: Burns from hot glassware or hot solution spitting out of the evaporating basin.
safety.precaution: Heat gently using a water bath, stop heating before the solution dries out, and use tongs to move the evaporating basin.

safety.risk: Burns, and fire if loose hair or clothing gets near the flame.
safety.precaution: Tie back hair, use a heatproof mat and turn the flame to the safety flame when not heating.

results.notes: 40 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid contains 0.040 mol H₂SO₄, so the maximum (theoretical) mass of hydrated copper sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O (Mr 249.5), is 0.040 × 249.5 = 9.98 g. The student obtained 7.49 g, a percentage yield of (7.49 ÷ 9.98) × 100 = 75.1%. Some copper sulfate is always left in the remaining solution and on the apparatus.

analysis: The black copper(II) oxide dissolved and the solution turned blue, showing that a reaction occurred and copper sulfate was formed: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l).

When black solid remained however much the mixture was stirred, all the acid had reacted. Using excess base means the final solution contains no unreacted acid, so the crystals are not contaminated with sulfuric acid.
Filtration removed the insoluble excess copper(II) oxide, leaving a solution that contained only copper sulfate and water. Crystallisation then separated the copper sulfate from the water.

The yield of crystals (75.1%) was less than 100% because some copper sulfate stayed dissolved in the solution left in the dish, some solution soaked into the filter paper, and some was lost when transferring between containers.

Heating the solution to dryness would give a powder rather than crystals and could decompose the hydrated salt (it turns white as water of crystallisation is lost), which is why the solution is only partly evaporated and then left to crystallise.

errors.error: Not enough copper(II) oxide added, so some sulfuric acid is left unreacted and contaminates the crystals.
errors.improvement: Keep adding copper(II) oxide until solid clearly remains after stirring for a minute; the excess guarantees all the acid has reacted.

errors.error: Solution lost when transferring between beaker, filter funnel, flask and evaporating basin, lowering the yield.
errors.improvement: Rinse each container with a small amount of distilled water and add the washings to the next container.

errors.error: Heating the solution too strongly or to dryness causes spitting and makes white anhydrous copper sulfate powder instead of blue crystals.
errors.improvement: Heat gently over a water bath, stop when crystals form on a cold glass rod, and let the rest of the water evaporate slowly at room temperature.

errors.error: Crystals still wet when weighed, so the measured mass is too high.
errors.improvement: Pat dry between filter papers, then leave in a warm place and weigh repeatedly until the mass is constant.

examTips: Learn the four stages in order: react (with the solid in excess), filter, evaporate (partly), crystallise.
Explain why the base is added in excess: to make sure all the acid reacts, so the salt is not contaminated with acid. The excess is easy to remove because it is insoluble.
Know how you can tell the base is in excess: solid stays at the bottom and will not dissolve (for a carbonate, fizzing also stops).
Do not heat to dryness: say that you heat until crystals start to form (or half the water has gone), then leave to cool and crystallise slowly.
Name the salt from the acid: sulfuric acid gives sulfates, hydrochloric acid gives chlorides and nitric acid gives nitrates.

questions.question: Which salt is made when copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper sulfate
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid always produces sulfate salts. A sulfide contains only sulfur and a metal, and chlorides come from hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: State how a student can tell that the copper(II) oxide has been added in excess.
markScheme: 1 mark: black solid remains / no more solid dissolves (even after stirring)
questions.explanation: When the acid has all been used up, extra copper(II) oxide has nothing to react with, so it stays as a black solid in the beaker.

questions.question: Explain why the copper(II) oxide is added in excess.
acceptedAnswers: no acid left in the salt
markScheme: 1 mark: to make sure all the (sulfuric) acid reacts / is used up
1 mark: so the salt is not contaminated with acid / the excess solid is insoluble so it can be removed by filtration
questions.explanation: Any acid left over would end up in the crystals. Because copper(II) oxide is insoluble, the leftover solid is easy to remove, so using too much does no harm.

questions.question: Which technique is used to remove the excess copper(II) oxide from the mixture?
markScheme: 1 mark: filtration
questions.explanation: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Crystallisation is used later to get the salt out of solution, and distillation would collect the water rather than the salt.

questions.question: Why is the sulfuric acid warmed before the copper(II) oxide is added?
options: To evaporate some of the water
To make the copper oxide soluble in water
To change the salt that is made
To increase the rate of the reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: to increase the rate of reaction / make the reaction faster
questions.explanation: Copper(II) oxide reacts slowly with cold acid. Warming speeds up the reaction. It does not change the product or make copper oxide dissolve in water.

questions.question: A student heated the copper sulfate solution in the evaporating basin until it was completely dry. Give two reasons why this is not a good idea.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: hot solution spits out (risk of burns); forms a powder or very small crystals instead of large crystals; hydrated copper sulfate loses its water of crystallisation and turns white (decomposes)
questions.explanation: The aim is pure, well-formed crystals. Partial evaporation followed by slow cooling gives larger crystals and avoids overheating the salt.

questions.question:
Complete the word equation for the reaction:
copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + ________
markScheme: 1 mark: water
questions.explanation: A metal oxide plus an acid gives a salt and water. No gas is produced (carbon dioxide only forms if a carbonate is used; hydrogen only with a metal).

questions.question: A student uses copper(II) carbonate instead of copper(II) oxide. What extra observation would show when the carbonate is in excess?
options: Fizzing stops when more carbonate is added
markScheme: 1 mark: fizzing / effervescence stops (and solid remains)
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acids to give carbon dioxide gas, which causes fizzing. When the acid has all reacted, adding more carbonate produces no more bubbles.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of copper sulfate, CuSO₄.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16
questions.explanation: Mr = 63.5 + 32 + 64 = 159.5. A common error is to add 16 only once instead of four times for the four oxygen atoms.

questions.question:
The maximum (theoretical) mass of copper sulfate crystals that could be made was 9.98 g. The student obtained 7.49 g.
Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100 = (7.49 ÷ 9.98) × 100 = 75.050%, which is 75.1% to 3 significant figures. Dividing the wrong way round gives a value over 100%, which is impossible.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why the mass of crystals obtained was less than the maximum possible mass.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: some copper sulfate remains dissolved in the solution that did not crystallise; some solution soaked into or stuck to the filter paper; solution lost when pouring between containers / left on the apparatus
questions.explanation: Yields are never 100% in practice because of losses during separation and because some salt stays in solution.

questions.question: Which pair of reactants could be used to make a pure, dry sample of zinc chloride by this method?
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc oxide and hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Chlorides are made from hydrochloric acid. Zinc oxide is an insoluble base so the excess can be filtered off. Sulfuric acid would give zinc sulfate and nitric acid would give zinc nitrate.

questions.question: Which is the correct balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction in this practical?
markScheme: 1 mark: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: Copper(II) oxide is an insoluble solid and copper sulfate stays dissolved in the solution. The products are a salt and water, not hydrogen, and the equation is balanced with 1 : 1 ratios.

questions.question: Explain why this method cannot be used to make sodium sulfate from sodium hydroxide and sulfuric acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium hydroxide is soluble (in water)
1 mark: so excess cannot be seen or removed by filtration; a titration must be used to find the exact volumes to mix
questions.explanation: This method relies on the base being insoluble, so the excess shows as a solid and can be filtered off. With a soluble alkali the excess would stay in solution and contaminate the salt.

questions.question:
Describe how to make a pure, dry sample of copper sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
Your answer should include the apparatus you would use.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure a volume of sulfuric acid (for example 40 cm³) with a measuring cylinder into a beaker; warm the acid gently with a Bunsen burner (do not boil); add copper(II) oxide a spatula at a time and stir; continue until black solid remains (excess); filter using filter funnel and filter paper to remove excess copper(II) oxide; collect blue filtrate in a conical flask or evaporating basin; heat gently (water bath) to evaporate some of the water until crystals form on a cold glass rod; leave to cool and crystallise; remove crystals and dry between filter papers or in a warm place; wear eye protection

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method covering reaction with excess oxide, filtration, partial evaporation and crystallisation, and drying, that would produce pure, dry crystals.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most stages described, but with some detail missing or out of order (for example no mention of excess or of how the crystals are dried).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple relevant statements, such as mix copper oxide with acid and heat, with little detail or logical order.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers name each stage and say why it is done: excess so all the acid reacts, filter to remove the excess, evaporate only partly so crystals form, then dry the crystals.
